Whereas, It is the earnest desire of the people of the Territory of Dakota residing south of the forty-sixth parallel that such part of said Territory should be formed into a State and admitted into the Union; and whereas, N. B. T. CAMPELL, Chairman.

EUGENE HUNTINGTON, Secretary.

Feb. 9, 1882.

The delegation, numbering about seventy members, called upon the president, and after formally presenting the matter for his consideration, retired with the understanding that he would meet a committee to-day. The committee, consisting of Maj. Kellam, chairman, Maj. Washburne, Messrs. Taylor, Cook and Sterling, called on the president to-day and had a full and satisfactory hearing.

THANKING PETTIGREW.

At a meeting of the delegates from North Dakota the following resolution was unanimously adopted:

Resolved, That the thanks of Northern Dakota are due and hereby tendered the Hon. R. F Pettigrew for his valuable aid in presenting the claims of that section of Dakota to a separate Territorial government, and for the uniform kindness and courtesy shown by him to the delegation.

Resolved, further, That this preamble and resolution be signed by the chairman and secretary of the delegation and that a copy thereof be presented to Mr. Pettigrew.

A. H. BARNES, Chairman,

F. H. ADAMS, Secretary.

Joseph Budd, in jail at Yankton for the murder of C. A. Borst, four years ago has been released on his own recognizance, pending the arrival of two important witnesses.

A negro barber broke into the residence of Mrs. Merrill of Watertown and attempted to rape her, but her cries brought asistance and the negro fled. A posse of citizens are after him and if caught will be dealt with in a summary inner.

It is intimated that Strang of Pennsylvania will succeed John B. Raymond as marshal of Dakota.

At Sioux Falls, a dwelling upon Phillips avenue, owned by Mrs. Schuntzeler and occupied by Edward Burns, was burned. Loss, $600; insured for $150.

Yankton Press: The Milwaukee road is making preparations to extend south beyond Ashton in the early spring, to connect at Huron with its Jim River branch from Yankton north. The great majority appear to be intelligent and in very comfortable circumstances—just the kind to make the Jim River prairies blossom beautifully.

A Washington special says that the proposition to establish a new land district in Dakota, with office at Jamestown, has every prospect of success.

Alexander H. Stevens says he will support measures for the division and admission of Dakota. He takes a broad and statismanlike view of the question.

In sinking a well on the tarm of Mr. Moore, twelve miles from Wahpeton, at the depth of 175 feet was struck a vein of water which thruws a full round stream twenty feet in the air, forming, as it wore, the finest artesian well in the great northwest.

A crazy fireman on the Northern Pacific freight train, near Alsop, recently, overpowered the engineer and undertook to run the train to suit his own idea of speed—about a mile a minute. The engineer finally succeeded in stopping the train just in time to save a collision, but had his coat and vest torn off by the maniac. As soon as the train was stopped the lunatic started across the prairie and has not since been seen.

Wm. A Moore has sold his paper, the Ordway (Dak.) Times, to Messrs. Elliott & Howard.

Ole Oleson Tol of Flandrau was kicked by a horse on Wednesday and died the following day.

Lawrence county has a debt of $550,000, which costs 10 per cent. interest.

Dell Rapids hopes to have 1,000 inhabitants before the end of the year.

The verdict of Justice Lawrence seems to meet the general approval of the people of Casselton.

LOS ANGELES, August 221.—An altercation occurred at Santa Monica Saturday between G. Scammon, of this city, and W. H. Gayner, of Santa Monica, in which the former gave the latter a few gashes with a knife upon the leg and face. None of the wounds are of a serious character. Sunday afternoon Max Newmark and wife, of Compton, were out enjoying a ride on the roads, above Old Santa Monica, leading to the bee ranches. They were accompanied by Mrs. Mallette, Mrs. Dillon and Miss Carpenter. While driving along about 6 P.M. the buggy was suddenly overturned and all were thrown to the ground. Serious Runaway Accident.

MERGED, August 22d.—An Italian fruit and vegetable peddler from the Badger Flat settlement, on the West Side, named Antonio, met with a serious accident here about 11 o'clock this morning. He had disposed of his load and started home, and after passing the El Capitan Hotel the hit came out of the mouth of one of his horses, when the team commenced to run. Not knowing what was the matter, Antonio pulled hard upon the lines, causing the team to run in a circle, and finally the horses broke across the railroad track, and on striking the rails threw the unfortunate man out, his head striking the rail of the track and tearing his scalp from the skull. He now lies at the Eagle Hotel in a precarious condition, though his skull does not seem to be fractured.

Result of Carelessly Handling a Pistol.

SMARTSVILLE, August 22d.—While Gus Moore was engaged in loading a pistol in the presence of his wife and children to-day, it was accidentally discharged, one bullet entering his thigh, inflicting a severe wound. Two others exploded a large can of powder, setting fire to his clothes and burning him and a six-year-old boy very severely.

Tragedy in Tulare County.

VISALIA, August 22d.—Ben Harris (colored) about 1 o'clock shot and mortally wounded his wife a mile north of town, killed a step-daughter aged 14 years, and struck in the forehead another step-daughter aged 10, but the child had hold of the handle of the ax and was too close to receive more than a slight wound in the forehead. He made his escape before the news reached town. Twenty or thirty men are on his trail and he may be caught before morning.

Window.

FRESNO, August 22d.—The public school-
house at the California Lumber Company's mill was destroyed by fire on the 17th. The fire is supposed to have been set by one of the students—a half-breed Indian girl.

A lamp exploded in the show-window of Maxe & Faber's store, in the Denahoe block, last evening, and destroyed the contents of the window before it was extinguished. The flames gained such headway that at one time it was thought a general conflagration would ensue. The loss is about $100.

Suicide of a Lunatic.

NAPA, August 22d.—George Alexander, aged 35 years, a patient at the Iosane Asylum, last night committed suicide by cutting his throat with a butcher knife.

Robbery on the Highway.

ORLAND, August 22d.—At about 8 o'clock last night the brewery-man of Germantown, while on his way from Riceville to this place, was knocked out of his wagon and robbed of twenty-eight dollars in money. There is no clue to the robbers, but they are supposed to have been tramps.

Sentence of the Tumor Fraud.

SAN DIEGO, August 22d.—Mrs. Dr. Patterson, the spiritualistic "tumor snatcher," was yesterday sentenced to pay a fine of $225 and serve six months in the County Jail.

A Fair Chance of Life.

FRESNO, August 22d.—Hensley, who was shot on Friday by Walter Brown, has so far rallied that his recovery is very probable. Brown was released on bail.

Sentence of a Forger.

NEVADA, August 22d.—In the Superior Court to-day Fred, Hinckley, who pleaded guilty Saturday to a charge of forgery, was sentenced to three years' imprisonment in the State Prison at Folsom.

Pork Townsend, August 23.—A man named Doyle, second mate on the steamer Mississippi, fell from between decks to the lower hold of that vessel while discharging freight here, and was badly injured. He was taken to the Marine Hospital for treatment.

The Queen.
SAN FRANCISCO, Aug. 23.—The steamer Queen of the Pacific will discharge at dan Louis Obispo about seven hundred tons of railroad iron. She is expected to arrive here about the 30th inst.

Murdered Three.
VISALIA, Cala., Aug. 23.—B. F. Harris, a colored man, living near here, shot and mortally wounded his wife, killed a step-daughter 14 years old, and seriously wounded another step-daughter, aged 10, with an axe. Harris escaped before rows of the tragedy reached town. Thirty men are in hot pursuit of the murderer.

Political Platform.
TUCSON, Aug. 23.—The following is a synopsis of the Republican platform adopted today at the Republican Territorial Convention: It declares allegiance to the national Republican platform of 1880; holds that all railroad and other corporations should be subject to the people through the Legislature; declares in favor of maintaining free public instruction; holds appropriations for the support of hostile Indians is a great wrong, and that hostile tribes should not be kept, fed and supported by the public treasury, and is in favor of disearning them; it declares against Chinese immigration and a free system of public offices; it claims that reorganization of the judicial system is necessary; demands that the Territorial and Federal Legislature should be used to discourage mining litigation, and to render mining titles more secure; declares in favor of free and unlimited coinage of silver upon the same terms and under the same regulations as gold.

FOREIGN.

In a single province of the Philippine islands 4,000 have died of cholera.

A decisive battle is expected to take place at Zagazig. The Egyptians lost 4,000 men in the recent battle. It is reported that Arabi is losing ground in the interior. Two thousand Albanians have been enlisted for service in hospitals. De Lesseps still thinks Arabi is a patriot, and prophesies British disaster. Dufferin adheres to his policy that Turkish troops shall only land at Rosetta, Damietta and Aboukir. General Wolseley has applied for more troops.

Three lepers have been found in Los Angeles.

There is no truth in the report of a revolution in Sonora.

Burns, Deputy Sheriff of Pascal, N. M., was shot at Silver City Saturday.

Thomas Williams was killed and three other miners were badly wounded by a cave in a Grass Valley mine Saturday.

The City Marshal of Nevada City has issued a notice to several hangers on at houses of bad repute to leave town on Monday or suffer the consequences. Among those thus notified are two or three parties who have been employed as piano-players.

The negro Harris, who murdered his family on Tuesday last, was found two and a half miles north of Visalia Saturday, at noon, and while attempting to escape he was shot by John Dice fatally. He had come to the house where he committed the murders during the night and was tracked to the place of rendezvous and killed. He will be buried in grave.

An informal meeting of the Cabinet was held at President Arthur's house in New York on the 21st. All the members, except Secretary Teller and Postmaster-General Howe, were present. There was no business transacted, and the session was more of a social one than otherwise. The cause of the meeting, as explained by Secretary Folger and Attorney-General Brewster, was that as Secretaries Lincoln, Chandler and Folger and the President were in New York, Secretary Frelinghuysen in Newark and Attorney-General Brewster at Long Branch, it was thought best to meet and inquire whether anything in any of the departments required joint action. FOUR chirus elephants escaped from their keepers in Troy, N. Y., Aug. 2. Patrick Ryan and wife were knocked down, the former receiving fatal injuries. Several other persons were hurt. One of the animals charged a bloom of red-hot iron in a rolling-mill.

BISHOP EMBERTON and Richard Speakman, who so brutally assaulted Mrs. J. B. Garrett, of Tompkinsville, Ky., a few days ago, were lynched by a mob, Aug. 1, while on the way to Glasgow under a guard of fifteen men.

The engine and mail car of a Union Pacific train went through a burned bridge spanning Granite Creek, between Glen Elder and Cawker City, Kans., Aug. 3. Britton Craft, engineer, and C. McGee, fireman, were fatally injured and died soon after. Mahaffy, express messenger, and Wentworth and Chamberlain, mail agents, were hurt, but not dangerously. W. H. Yeates was hanged at Chatham, Va., Aug. 4, for the murder of P. E. Adkerson. Two negroes mounted the scaffold in Florida on the same day: Merrick Jackson, at Fernandina, and Harrison Carter, at Jacksville.

At Indianapolis, the other evening, two colored boys, Charles Bly and James Jones, engaged in a friendly sparring match. Bly was struck in the stomach and expired before medical aid could be secured.

There are many bad characters in town. In fact we have as many hoodlums here now as we had three years ago, when we found it necessary to hang two of them by lynch law. It seems that there are many who sympathize with the miscreants who were arrested yesterday. To all such we say—and we are backed up by all the law abiding citizens of Phoenix—that the sooner they make themselves scarce, the better for their worthless carcasses. No more hoodlums will be tolerated in our town, and the men referred to will do well to leave pretty shortly, for they are known and watched. It will only be a few more days until this matter will be carefully looked after by the authorities, and should they fail, the citizens themselves will take care of it. The saloons are filled with men who do nothing for their living, and yet have money to spend. How do they get it? No one knows. Probably by "rolling" some poor drunk who happens to have money in his pocket, or by some other devilry. We endorse the action of our city Marshal in yesterday's fuss, and congratulate ourselves that we were so fortunate as to have such an officer. If Tombstone or Calabasas have any more cowboys to spare let them send them to Phoenix and we will take charge of them.

THE MINNEAPOLIS PLAN.
A Negro Ravisher in Ohio Hung by Indignant Citizens on the Spot Where His Terrible Crime Was Committed—Louisville Furnishes Another Victim.

CLEVELAND, Ohio, April 30.—A Galion dispatch says: The negro ravisher Fisher, was captured at five o'clock this morning at Frederickstown, Knox county, by two officers, just as he was leaving this place afoot. Fisher denied his name but was recognized, arrested and taken in a carriage to Galion, where he was put in an iron cage in the city prison about noon, arrangements being made to send him to a jail in some neighboring county to prevent threatened lynching, but at 3 o'clock a large crowd of determined people unmasked, went boldly up to the city hall prison and demanded the surrender of the negro to them. The officers refused and Mayor Underwood and others made speeches to the excited throng, counseling that the law be permitted to take its course, but to no purpose.

The mob forced the doors of the prison, broke down the iron cage and dragged the negro into the street with fierce shouts. Meanwhile a delegation accompanied by physicians who had been pressed into the service, drove to the house of the victim of the negro's lust to ascertain whether the girl, Barbara Rettie, was morally and physically able to confront and identify the prisoner. She told the physician she could as she had often seen him chopping wood near her home. This being reported to the crowd the negro was marched to her home, preceded by men carrying a rope, and surrounded by a howling rabble. When Barbara saw the cowering wretch, she exclaimed: "That is the man," and fainted.

The noose was then thrown over the negro's head and he was dragged to a tree at the rear of the lot. Somebody suggested the scene of the rape was the fittest place to strangle him. This was the view of all, and Fisher was taken to the spot, when he was told that his time had come to die. He protested his innocence to the last, but the blood still perceptible on his clothing was evidence of guilt, as well as the girl's statement, and he was quickly strung up, when the crowd quietly dispersed.

JUDGE LYNCH ACTS.
The Black Brute Who Outraged a Child at Galion Hanged by the People.
GALION, O., May 1.—Last Friday as Barbara Rettig, a German girl, thirteen years of age, was returning home from a neighbor's house, she was assaulted by Frank Fisher, a burly negro, dragged into the woods, repeatedly and brutally outraged, and left in an insensible condition. When she returned to consciousness and dragged herself home and told her story, there was intense excitement, and searching parties were immediately organized to look for the black beast and capture him if possible. Yesterday morning a negro answering to the girl's description was arrested in Frederickstown, Knox county, and brought here and lodged in jail. Immediately a crowd began to gather, and ominous threats of lynching were heard. The fire bells were sounded, whistles blown, and the people began to gather around the jail. The officers in charge of the jail were unprepared for an assault, and tried to induce the mob to leave. The Mayor also addressed the mob, advising order and counseling them to let the law take its course. All pleadings were vain. A rush was made, the jail doors forced, the prisoner's cell broken into, and the hapless wretch dragged out, howling and begging for mercy. The people seemed frenzied with fury, and the prisoner was dragged along the street, kicked, choked, and pelted with stones at every step. The negro was taken to the home of the injured girl and taken into her presence as she lay suffering the most intense pain, and unable to move. She was asked if the prisoner was the man who misused her, and she said, without hesitation, that he was the man. There was other and conclusive evidence against him, and he was told that his time had come to die. He was taken from the house and followed by a howling mob of at least two thousand people, dragged to the woods where his foul crime was committed, and bidden to make his peace with God, for his time was short. The scene was horrible. Fisher, with distorted face, shrieked for mercy and protested his innocence. He was told he could have five minutes to pray, but all the more he writhled and twisted and asked for mercy. To the very last he delared his innocence. When the five minutes were expired the hands of the shrieking wretch were pinioned, a rope was placed around his neck and the other end thrown over the limb of a tree. There was a moment's pause, and a pitiful scream of the victim was stifled as the rope was pulled up and he swung writhing in mid air. The crowd stood by until the last convulsive struggles were over, and then disappeared, leaving the body hanging, and where it remained all night. There are but few people who condemn the deed, however lawless, and the general sentiment is that it was well done.

LYNCHED.
Frank Fisher Taken From the Gallon Jail and Hanged.

GALION, Ohio, April 30, 1882.

This has been the most exciting day in the history of the city and county. Frank Fisher, the negro who so horribly outraged the little German girl, Barbara Rettig, aged only thirteen years, in the woods, where he had been chopping wood last Friday noon, and who escaped, was captured about five o'clock this morning at Fredericktown, Knox County, by Officers T. J. Wurts and W. H. W. Nichols, of this city. The arrest was made just as the negro was about to leave Fredericktown on foot. He was first accosted by Officer Wurts, who asked him whether his name was Frank Fisher. "No, sah, that is not my name, sah," he replied, but Officer Nichols knew him, and after a few more questions, among which was asked why he had left Galion, he replied that he had got tired of chopping wood and thought he would skip. The officers, of course, arrested him, and at once started with him in a carriage, accompanied by two Fredericktown officers, for this city, arriving here at 11:30 this morning. The prisoner was at once taken to the jail in the City Hall and confined in one of the heavy iron cages, and the Mayor and city officers were laying plans to take him to the county jail at Bucyrus, or some other jail in some neighboring county, fearing that the loud threats of lynching would be carried out if Fisher would remain in the City Hall cell. Their fears were well founded, for the news of Fisher's capture spread through the city and the neighboring town like wild-fire, and at three o'clock this afternoon a large crowd of determined men boldly, defiantly and unmasked, with hammers, crowbars and other implements, and a huge and significant loop-rope, presented themselves before the entrance of the City Hall prison and demanded that Frank Fisher, the negro rapist, be surrendered into their hands. The officers of course refused. Then ensued a terrible scene of strife. The handful of officers were powerless, and the speeches of Mayor Underwood, G. M. Zeigler and others, who begged the excited crowd to let the law take its course and deal with the prisoner whose blood they sought, were unavailing and unheeded. With their implements of destruction they forced open the doors as though they were paper, broke open the iron cage that contained the guilty, trembling wretch, and grasping him with a dozen hands, as in a vise, they pulled him out into the street with a defiant shout. Previous to this, however, a delegation accompanied by a physician, whom they had pressed into service, drove furiously down to the residence of the victim of the negro's lust to ascertain whether she was in a proper mental and physical condition to see the negro for identification. The physician states to your correspondent that he asked her whether she knew the negro who had caused her misery. She replied yes, that she had often seen him while he was chopping wood near their home, and described his appearance. Being asked whether she could identify him, she replied she could. The delegation being satisfied reported at the City Hall, and then the scene that has been described was enacted. With hoots, yells and cheers, the crowd, preceded by some men and boys, bearing the fatal rope, marched with the frightened negro to the Rettig residence, at the foot of South Market Street, just south of the city limits, and took the black beast into the presence of Barbara Rettig, the little girl whom he had so horribly outraged. As soon as her eyes fell upon the cowardly and cowering wretch before her, she exclaimed: "That is the man who did it," and soon fainted with the terrible recollections.

The crowd threw the rope over the negro's head and dragged him to a tree in the rear of the lot, but some one suggested the woods—the scene of his terrible crime—hard by as the fit place to expiate his crime, and to the woods where he had been but a few pays ago chopping wood Frank Fisher was dragged and told that his time to die had come. Mr. Scoville and his wife, while in Milwaukee on Saturday, to arrange for the repurchase of some property, which had been foreclosed under a mortgage, had a bitter quarrel in the presence of the lawyer. The Egyptian Crisis.

OBJECT OF THE ALEXANDRIA RIOTERS.

LONDON, June 12.—Advices from Alexandria late last night state that the disturbances commenced simultaneously at three different points. The object of the rioters in a great measure appears to have been pillage, in which Levantines, as well as Arabs, participated. A regiment of cavalry and a regiment of infantry have been ordered to reinforce the garrison.

SIXTY-SEVEN EUROPEANS KILLED.

A telegram published in London says: The official report of the riot in Alexandria gives the number of Europeans killed as 67. Arabi Pacha and Mahmoud Pachi Saml had separate interviews with Dervisch Pacha yesterday. The result of the interview is not known, but it is generally believed that they submit to Dervisch Pacha's views.

CONTINUED EXCITEMENT IN ALEXANDRIA.

ALEXANDRIA, Monday morning.—Great excitement continues; all the shops are closed.

MORE ABOUT THE RIOTS—THE ENGINEER OF THE SUPERB KILLED.

LONDON, June 12.—The admiralty have received dispatches confirming the report of the murder of the engineer of the Superb. The fighting at Alexandria, expert the deliberate attack upon the consuls when proceeding to the residence of the governor, seems to have been confined to Arabs and Levantines. No English resident is reported to have been wounded.

The Times' correspondent at Cairo lays the responsibility for the riot upon Arabi Pacha. Dervisch Pacha had summoned him to resign, and there seemed to be no alternative but submission or defiance, but since the riots broke out Dervisch Pacha has had to appeal to Arabi Pacha, as commanding the only available force, to restore order.

LONDON, June 12.—A dispatch to the Standard from Pesth states that a disastrous flood has occurred at Versez owing to a sudden rising of the river. A number of houses and two bridges were destroyed. Twelve children and several adults were drowned.

GEN. IGNATIEFF BELIEVED.

St. PETERSBURG, June 12.—A decree is published announcing that Gen. Ignatieff, at his own request, has been relieved of the post of minister of the interior, on the ground of ill-health, and has been appointed president of the academy and a member of the senate. GAMBETTA TO VISIT ENGLAND.

LONDON, June 12.—The Times says M. Gambetta is likely to visit England next week.

Cohoes, N.Y., June 12.—Five weavers went to work in the Harmony mill, to-day, under the ten per cent reduction. Great excitement prevails. Three thousand strikers are gathered about the mill gates, and threats are made to kill the seceders. The entire police force have been put on guard.

St. Louis, Mo., June 12.—A special to the Republican from Kirksville says: The wife of Frank Mason, the leader of the bank robbers, has delivered up $1,600 in gold, stolen from the Brookfield bank. WINNIPEG, Man., June 12.—Ross resumed his training on the Red river to-day. He will claim the championship, as Hanlan fails on his second deposit.

Advices from New Mexico are to the effect that Deputy Sheriff Miers and Martinez with a posse were attacked by Pueblo Indians while attempting to arrest some of the Pueblos who had escaped from jail. Miers was killed and Martinez mortally wounded.

A shocking tragedy took place at Boston, Mass., on the 7th inst. Mrs. Harriet Bell while returning from a grocery store near her home was accosted by an unknown man who followed her to the doorstep of her home and then cut her throat. She lived but a short time. The assassin escaped.

A brace of cattle thieves named Arnold Howard and Frank Young, in jail at Del Noter, Col., were visited by a mob on the 7th inst. Howard was killed outright and Young mortally wounded.

An affray with pistols took place at Arkansas City, on the 5th inst., in which J. W. Hale was killed by John Fuller.

Three negroes—Lewis Smith and Aaron and Ed. Clark—were killed in an affray at Arkadelphia, Ark., on the 6th inst. The shooting was done by Joe Ross and Thad. Henry, both white.

Tax Collector Robert Taylor was shot dead by Dr. Sims at Perryville, Perry County, Ark., on the 4th inst.

Georgia Affairs.
The Perry Home Journal says that at an early date there will be a chicken fight in Perry. All the cocks will be placed in the pit at once, and the owner of the last one to leave the pit takes all the other chickens as the prize of the victor.

The brick work on Seney Hall, at Oxford, is nearly complete; the slating has been put on three sides of the roof, and a good deal of the outside ornamental work finished. The work will go on rapidly now, and be complete by the first of July, at all events.

In Wild-cat di-trict, Forsyth county, last Sunday morning, William James shot a man just above the left nipple, the ball ranging downward and coming out under the shoulder blade.

Albany News and Advertiser: "The steam gin and grist mill of Mr. Sam. W. Livingston, of Newton, was destroyed by fire on Sunday night. The origin of the fire is supposed to have been incendary. The loss is estimated at $30,00. We are unable to state whether there was any insurance on the property or not."

Albany News and Advertiser: "Calvin, the old blind colored man, who pumps water at the Savannah, Florida and Western Railway tank in this city, met with a most unfortunate accident on Sunday. He fell between the depot platform and a box car and broke his leg in two places. He is in great pain, and it is hardly probable that he will ever be able to work any more."

Atlanta Post Appeal: "There is an important gathering of railroad magnates in the city at present, all of the lessees of the State Road being either here or represented. The object of this assemblage is a thorough discussion of the situation in view of the recent decision by Attorney General Anderson. A meeting was held Saturday and another will take place this evening. It is learned that no idea of abandoning the lease is entertained, and any effort to set it aside by the State authorities will be strenuously resisted."

Clayton, remembers distinctly when the Oconee river used to run down Broad street. This aged colored man says that he had a fish hole under the large sycamore trees where the National Bank now stands, and that he helped to ditch above Lincoln's plantation, and turn the river in its present channel. Thomaston correspondent Constitution: "Alice McCoy, colored, boarded the train en route to Barnesville from here, and when Conductor Hammond came around he found Alice in the ladies car, and tellin her to get out she refused. Mr. Hammond then ordered her taken out by the Marshal. Mr. Arnold Anderson, who happened to be at the depot. Alice is the mother of Jesse and Whit, two boys who were sent to the chain gang from here last year for breaking in the store of Joseph Allen & Co., on Main street."

Chronicle and Constitutionalist: "Work on King Factory is progressing rapidly. Workmen are busily employed in all directions in breaking, leveling and hauling the ground where it will soon rear itself alongside the Sibley Mills. The foundation of the principal building will soon be completed. There are also in operation two brick molds. They both turn out about 50,000 brick daily. The clay is first wet and fed into the molds on one side as mud and comes out on the other side made into the form of bricks. They are then piled in rows, and after having been thoroughly dried by the sun, are put in the kins and subjected to a great heat for about five days, and then allowed to cool, and are afterwards taken out ready for being used to form the walls of the factory."

Atlanta Post-Appeal: "W. S. Wilson & Bro., coal and lumber dealers on Spring street, exhibited a shattered safe to a reporter this morning which showed the skill of an artist in safe burglary. A hole was drilled near the combination, filled with powder, the fastening blown asunder and the contents of the safe left to the mercy of the depreyders. They riffed the drawers and took the little iron box from its fastening, and going out to the lumber yard tipped it open with a chisel and scooped in its contents, leaving the box and a small drawer contained in it on a lumber pile. The Messrs Wilson are somewhat reticent as to the amount contained in the box, but state that there were fifty dollars in the drawer and a number of checks, which latter were left. The box may have contained one hundred or five hundred dollars. An entrance to the office was effected through the door, which offered little resistance. No cue was left as to who the thief or thieves were. It would be well, while these safe burglars are sojourning with us, for those who have no burglar proof safe to deposit their valuables in a vault for safety."

Monroe Advertiser: "The store of Mr. R. M. Williams, at iceberg, was entered and robbed last Thursday night. The store is set upon a rock foundation. This was broken through and the burglaries thereby got into the cellar and had no difficulty in entering the store therefrom. A large quantity of goods was stolen—value of which cannot well be calculated. Several of the negro workmen on the railroad were arrested on suspicion Friday, and tried before a magistrate, but the proof was not strong enough to warrant their commitment. None of the goods have been found. On Saturday a white man, named A. S. Averitt, was arrested in Macon, as the burglar. He had sold of the stolen goods, and thus he was traced. Mr. Williams being notified of his arrest, sent Mr. Little to Macon after him. He confessed the crime to Mr. Little, and had already confessed to the policeman who arrested him. He was brought to Forsyth and is now in jail. He seems to be a respectable man, and expresses deep regret for his crime, says it is his first offense and shall be his last. He is from Futnam county, and was at work on the railroad, previous to his crime."

Augusta News, 11th: "A young boy was saved from drowning in the canal this morning through the timely arrival and heroic exertions of a gentleman passing near the scene on McKinne street, over the third level of the canal. The little fellow, John Hardman, who lives in that neighborhood, fell into the water while playing with some companions, about a hundred yards from McKinne street. Their exertions to rescue him as he floated down the stream, which is swift at that place, were confined to holding out sticks to him, and while grasping at them he was several times carried under the water. While drifting helplessly along and when about to fail in strength he was seen by Dr. Frank M. Deems, Mr. George Howard and one or two others passing along the street. The two gentlemen named jumped from their vehicles, rushed down the bank, and Dr. Deems, who was first at the water, called to Mr. Howard to stay on the bank and not to jump in unless necessary. Dr. Deems then plunged n the water and swam out to the little fellow, who was about to sink for the last time. With the grasp of a dying man, he seized Dr. Deems as he reached him, and both went under the water. Rising to the surface, the Doctor pushed for the bank with his burden, and was sssisted by Mr. Howard and his colored driver, Eugene. Both were pulled out of the water exhausted. Dr. Deems administered restoratives to the little fellow, and, after sending him home and going across the street to his own residence, nursed him until he was all safe."

The Constitution says: "Gen. P. M. B. Young will certainly be a candidate for Congress at large, and Judge J. W. H. Underwood will probably contest the mountain delegations with him."

An incorrigible little darkey, a thief from boyhood, of Walker county, named Andy Hall, only ten years old, was sentenced to the penitentiary of Dade coal pits for five years, at the recent session of the Superior Court in that county, for stealing a horse.

T. A. Bean, who deserted his wife at Newnan a few days ago and went to Atlanta with a depraved female, was tried at Newnan last Tuesday for wife desertion, found guilty and sentenced to the chain gang for 12 months.

Dublin Gazette: We learn that the candidates for the Legislature from this county, are as thick as the hairs on a dog's back. In fact, we learn that every man who can spell baker and give out an old fashioned hymn, is a candidate before the dear people.

James White, of Dalton, while preparing his gun for hunting last Friday, rested it upon a vat's edge, at White's tannery, to remove a wadding, and upon suddenly turning it fell into the vat, striking the hammer and discharging the gun in its decent. A load passed through White's left arm, grazing his side. The wounded member is much swollen and inflamed, and amputation will perhaps be necessary.

Commissioner Henderson said to a Constitution reporter: "The decrease in the sale of fertilizers this year is surprising. There has been less sold so far than for the same period at any time in the last eight years. The price varies in different localities, and in some places standard fertilizers sell as low as four hundred pounds of middling cotton per ton."

We have not as yet learned when operations will again commence. The car factory is working on full time, although without as many hands as before the explosion, the engine not being of sufficient power to work so many. Their new engine will probably arrive within a month.

We learn that the man, Peter Corbin, charged with committing an outrage on a lady in Gilmer county, who was arrested in this place week before last by deputy marshal King and turned over to the sheriff of said county, mention of which was made in this paper, was taken from the Gilmer county jail, the night after the sheriff returned to Ellijay with him, by a party of masked men and was found the next day in a piece of woods near the town with his head completely severed from his body. The two quarreled and one of them started for his gun, which was a short distance away, and the other drew his little pistol and shot at him twice, one ball striking him in the back and coming out just above the navel. He got his gun, but when he got back his antagonist had fled the field. When our informant left, a few hours after, the wounded man was dying. The murderer is still at large. We could not learn the names of the parties."

Meriwether Vindicator: "Charlie, son of Mr. W. P. Findley, has been spending several months at Senoia with his grandfather, Mr. J. B. Heard. Recently the boy ran down to the train to mail a letter. The letter being mailed, the little boy stepped back to the platform, and overcome by his exertion in running, as it is supposed, he swooped and fell to the ground, a distance of several feet. In falling his breast struck the end of a crosstie. Since that time Charlie has lost all appetite, and is frequently attacked with such paroxysms of pain as to render his screams almost heart-rending. He is carefully attended by Dr Brantley, who pronounced his case a most singular one."

Columbus Times: "Mr. Fred, Little, of Allen's Station, Richmond county, said in his essay at the Georgia Agricultural Convention, in Augusta: 'In his opinion the best land for watermelon culture was a sandy loam, and if possible, a place which had laid out for some time, and had grown up in small pines and broom sedge. He then proceeded to give his method of culture. When the plants are well established they should be thinned down to one plant to a hill if large melons are desired, and this is very requisite if the melons are intended for sale.' The most popular melon in this market the past season was the Mountain Sweet and a long white or gray rhind, and we hope the market gardeners will be prepared to supply the market with fine ones the present season, hence we publish the above."

He had engaged a horse from one of our livery stables for the purpose of going out into the country to see Mr. Mitchell. Just as he got opposite Messrs. King & Bros' store, the horse was moving at a pretty lively speed, when Mr. Neal, not wanting to go so fast, gave the rein a sudden jerk, the horse rearing up and falling backwards, throwing Mr. Neal to the ground. the swamps of Louisiana, until herds were driven from their fastnesses by the high water of the present season. In the immediate vicinity of Natchez there have been hundreds, and we may probably be speaking within bounds when we say thousands, of these beautiful animals, which have crossed the river within the space of a few miles above and below this city. Worn and exhausted as they have been, after their long swim across the swollen river, they would have fallen an easy prey to the pot-hunters who only hunt for profit, had it not been for the extraordinary exertions of the true sportsmen of the county, and humane people who despise wanton cruelty. On Sunday last, several gentlemen found a number of deer that had fallen into a ravine, from which they found it impossible to get out. With true humanity they went to work and dug a pathway by which the little animals could find their way out of the ravine, helped them to mount to the top of the bank, and sent them on their way rejoicing to the green woods of the country. Instances of the same kind of humane feeling have been, we are glad to say, the rule with the people of this vicinity, while the disposition to capture and kill the deer has been the exception. —Natchez Democrat.

At Burkeville, Newton County, Tex., there is on the premises of Judge M. D. Hines a well of ordinary width and depth, to obtain water from which two buckets are used. These are connected by a rope, which passes over a wheel suspended from a frame above the curbing. The contrivance is a simple one, the arrangements being such that as one bucket is drawn up the other descends. The strange feature about the well is that at irregular periods, and without any visible or known cause, the buckets will change places, the empty one descending to the bottom and the filled one rising to the top of the well.

Mrs. Coker, with her three children, in an ox-cart, was recently returning home from Perry, Ga. The road they traveled passed through very rank wire-grass, which had been set on fire. In trying to get out of the way the cart and oxen became fastened among pine logs, and the fire overtook them. The cart, with the two children inside, was consumed and the oxen were burned to death. The woman attempted to escape with her infant, but her clothing caught fire and she and the other child were so badly burned that they have since died.

A novel suit has been entered by a citizen of Atlanta, Ga. He has been unable, after two years of trial, to get a place in the public schools. He now proposes to resist the payment of the school-tax by law, and has employed an attorney to take the matter in hand. He says: "I do not see why I should be taxed to support the schools when I can not get any representation in them. I have the same right of any other citizen to send my boy, and yet there are hundreds of others who get schooling and I have none. I do not think they can collect a school-tax when they refuse to let me send my son to the school."

The owner of the cave deposits of bat guano in Uvalde County, Texas, says the supply can not be exhausted in a century. An analysis shows over 11 per cent. of ammonia. The caves have recently been reached by railroad tracks, and the first shipment has been made. The product is expected to bring $50 per ton.

For several months says the Conyers (Ga.) Weekly, one of our citizens has been noticing that his butcher invariably let his hand rest on the meat slightly when he weighed it, and he reweighed it at home and found it from a half to a pound short. He kept an account of these deficiencies, and when they aggregated one hundred pounds he took out an attachment for the butcher's hand, claiming that it rightly belonged to him, he having more than paid for it.

The region south of Memphis is swarming with buffalo-gnats, which are killing what little stock was saved from drowning.

The New Orleans Gas-Light Company has been declared by Judge Pardee to have no legal existence.

Out of a total vote of 640, Bryan, Tex., gave a majority of 377 for liquor prohibition.

A convicted horse-thief named Bondy jumped from a train near San Antonio, Tex., last week, and was shot dead by the guards.

Two negroes, who were resisting arrest for forgery, were shot by a constable at Morrow's Station, Ga., a few days ago. Both escaped, but one, named Bloom, was afterward found dead in the woods. The negroes had first shot at the constable.

One hundred families have moved into Birmingham, Ala., since the 1st of December.

Gov. Colquitt, of Georgia, has determined not to call an extra session of the Legislature for the purpose of redistricting the State.

Eighty-five thousand tons of fertilizers were sold in North Carolina for the year 1881.

Silk culture in Louisiana has of late become a thriving industry, and promises an abundant production.

In 1865 Florence, S. C., contained only ten houses. It now has a population of over 2,000, and last year over 100 houses were built.

A Justice of the Peace in Atascosa County, Texas, says that he has assessed but two fines for misdemeanors during eight years.

Watermelons are up and doing well in Georgia. Three hundred acres are planted in Brooks County.

Representative Black, of Georgia, is seriously ill. He is not expected to recover.

Macon, Ga., had a $50,000 fire the other day, and Mr. R. B. Watson, cotton broker, perished in the flames.
Floriada is full of tourists.

It has been developed upon investigation that labor bureaus are in active operation in Texas and Louisiana, which have been organized for the purpose of meeting the large demand made by sugar and cotton planters in those States for laborers.
Isidore Levy, of New Orleans, who was arrested for arson at the instance of the insurance companies and was acquitted, has brought suit against the underwriters for $100,000.
Faber gets the wood for his pencils from Cedar Keys, Fla.

A Former Dallas Hotel Waiter in Trouble for Killing at El Paso.
Information comes from El Paso that a few days ago in the Mexican section of that city, a colored man by the name of Riley Wiggins, known to many of the Grand-Windsor hotel boarders as Sam, Smiling Sam, something of a musician, killed two Mexicans there this week. The circumstances appear to be these: Sam was an assistant cook in one of the hotels, and had a difficulty with some of his fellows. Pistols were drawn on him when he started to run and escape, when the Mexican boys fired upon him wounding him in the head. He fired some shots and killed two of them. Sam is now in jail at El Paso, and they have tried to lynch him, though he is duly cared for by the officials in charge. A letter from one of his colored friends there, John McCutcheon, to Sam's former fellow-waiters at the Windsor here, says that inasmuch as he has to be tried in the Mexican limits, where the killing was done, he fears full justice will not be done, and he asks for some assistance from here. Sam, it seems, has a family or relatives in Mansfield, Louisiana.

Serious Accident.

ALTA, June 28th.—J. Henderson and J. P. Pollard, of Grass Valley, were thrown from a buggy while crossing the railroad here at 1 o'clock this afternoon. Henderson was badly bruised about the left temple, and sustained some serious flash wounds about the body. Pollard escaped without serious injury. Henderson at 8 P.M. is still unconscious, but his physician thinks the wounds not necessarily fatal. The accident was caused by the fractional team becoming frightened at a locomotive standing on the side track. The buggy is a wreck, and one horse was badly cut.

Fire—The Fraudulent Certificate Case.

NEVADA CITY, June 28th.—A fire yesterday on Aristocracy Hill, in this city, destroyed a barn and its contents belonging to Frank Guild, and some outhouses belonging to John Hook. The loss was about $650. There was no insurance.

The County Board of Education met yesterday for final action upon the case against Mary McAuliffe, Maggie Ryan and Ada Deacon, of Grass Valley, recently tried for unprofessional conduct by asking for and receiving information while writing for teachers' certificates. County Superintendent Hickes and Mr. Preston voted to revoke their certificates, while Messrs. Power, Byrne and Potter opposed the motion. Unprejudged outsiders, who heard the testimony, are surprised at the result. The subject will be revived in some shape when the County Supervisors meet.

Impressive Funeral Ceremonies.

NEVADA, June 28th.—The funeral ceremonies of George S. Powers, the deceased mining Superintendent, were held here today, under the auspices of the Nevada Commandery, Knights Templar, and were of a very impressive nature. Sir Knights were present from all parts of this Sierra, Placer and other counties. The remains were taken to the train and escorted to Colfax by a large delegation of Knights. Business generally was suspended during the progress of the ceremonies.

The Chico Wife Murderer Held to Answer.

OROVILLE, June 28th.—The preliminary examination of the Chico wife murderer, Schmidt, took place to-day at this place before Justice Leonard. The evidence disclosed an unprovoked and brutal killing, without any notice or warning whatever. He was held to answer without bonds on a charge of murder. He offered no evidence in his defense, and appeared for examination without counsel.

The Stranded Ship.

BODEGA, June 28th.—There are no reliable details from the wreck. The ship is hard and fast on the reef. The tide rises on her deck at high water, leaving her pretty well forward at low water. Portions of the top sail and top-gallant sails are still set. The steamer Santa Cruz took the Captain, officers and all hands to San Francisco this morning.

Body Recovered.

SAN RAPAEL, June 28th.—The body of George Reinfeld, the boy who was drowned with his two sisters by the upsetting of a boat near Saucelito last Sunday, was recovered to-day.

Death from Natural Causes—A 200-Foot Fall.

SAN JOSE, June 28th.—The inquest this evening on the body of Mrs. Isabella Dillon, found dead yesterday in her house on the Alameda, resulted in a verdict of death from natural causes.

At half-past 5 last evening Santiago Ordines, a Chilean miner, attempted to climb upon a hoisting cage while in motion in the Randal shaft of the Almaden quicksilver mine, and fell from the 1600 to the 1800 foot level, being instantly killed. OAKLAND, July 6th.—One of the most disastrous fires ever known in Berkeley occurred early this morning. The large hotel known as the "Olive Branch," situated on Choate street, at the terminus of the Oakland dummy railroad, was totally destroyed. The fire was discovered about 3 o'clock by some of the members of the Mackin family, living directly opposite on Choate street. The neighborhood was quickly aroused and a dozen or two men soon gathered and did all that was possible to prevent the spread of the flames. Rapid Judicial Proceedings.
OROVILLE, July 6th.—The Chico wife murderer Schmidt was to day sentenced by Judge Hundley to be hanged. THE FIRE DEPARTMENT. Chief Engineer Galligan Turns Over the Keys to His Successor.
Chief Engineer J. J. Galligan, who for seven years conducted the affairs of the fire department of this city, once for a term of three years and again for four and a half, yesterday surrendered his office, keys and mantle of authority to Capt. John H. Butler, who was nominated by the mayor and confirmed by the council Tuesday night as chief.

The appointment was in many respects unsatisfactory to the boys, it being admitted that the election of April 13th, which saw Mr. Edward Welsh chosen to the office, was a legal one, and the protest made being decidedly mild. Capt. Butler may be a number one man, and prove a good chief, but he will have hard work to fill the place Jack Galligan has occupied for so long. There probably never was a better fireman in Omaha; he was always on time, foremost in fighting the fire and ready to brave any danger however great. He never asked a man to go where he wouldn't go, and many a time has gone where others dared not. After the catastrophe of September 5th 1878, when the city got a serious lesson on the subject of appointing men whose skill was to be tested and was not already proven, it would seem that that would have been enough and it was asserted yesterday by firemen and others that the first emergency will see another transfer of the office like the one in 1878.

The boys of No. 2 are indignant at the rejection of their candidate, Mr. Welsh, and called a meeting for yesterday at which there was a prospect of a lively time. Some are for disbanding and retiring from the service, and it may be that the business will end in the total disorganization of the department. Certainly the effort to harmonize the two factions in the department is by no means successful and harmony seems farther off than ever. It is said that the mayor merely wishes to keep up his reputation for doing what nobody else would think of doing.

THE FIREMEN'S MEETING.

At 8 o'clock last evening there was quite a large gathering at Firemen's Hall, and the meeting was called to order by the president of No. 2, F. J. McShane, who stated the object of the meeting.

It appears that a company meeting was held in the morning, at which steps were taken to ascertain the amount of funds in the company treasury, and also in the department treasury, the idea being to pay Mr. Edward Welch the amount in which he was the loser in the campaign for the position of chief engineer of the department.

It was, in accordance with the determination of this meeting, moved, that the secretary be instructed to draw a warrant for $50 on the treasurer, to be paid over to Mr. Welch, and this motion was carried.

Messrs. O'Byrne, Ryan and Ed Kosters were appointed a committee to hand

handsome secretary's desk to the now in progress at Creighton hall, this representing their part of the furniture in Firemen's Hall. There was a number of old members present at the meeting who did not grasp the drift of things and could not understand what this move meant. The boys explained that the other companies had desks in the hall that they could use and they wanted to contribute to the fair, as there was no telling when one of them might be sent to the hospital.

The motion carried, and Messrs. Ed Kosters, Morris Hengen and Barney Shannon were appointed a committee to deliver the desk to the officers of the fair, and they did so on the adjournment of the meeting.

On motion the president was requested to appoint a committee of five to request the president of the department to call a general meeting as soon as possible, and the following were appointed as such committee: Barney Shannon, Jas. Teahon, I. W. Miner, Fred Lowe and Theo. Grebe.

The company then adjourned for two weeks.

Lynching in Henderson.
HENDERSON, July 12, 1882.

Henderson county is now to the front with a horrible tile of outrage and murder, and the now, in Kentucky, almost inevitable lynching. A week ago last Monday the friends of Helen Brewster, a colored girl about fourteen years of age, who lives in the Bellefield neighborhood, about six miles from this city, were greatly disturbed over her sudden and mysterious disappearance, and for several days could learn nothing that would furnish a clew to her whereabouts. On the morning of the day of her disappearance she was seen in company with William Ritter, a negro who farmed in a small way about a mile from the residence of Mr. Junius Taylor, where the Brewster girl worked, but his answers to all inquiries threw no light on her whereabouts. The search, however, availed nothing until last Sunday morning when Ritter, whose crime seemed to weigh heavily on his mind, announced the finding of a bonnet near a field in which he had been plowing, and this proved to be the one worn by the girl when last seen. Ritter's actions, coupled with several questions he asked, led to the belief that he knew more of the girl than he cared about telling, and after a search for and the finding of her body, he was arrested.

The body was found in the woods, not more than a hundred yards from the field, and was badly decomposed, yet still recognizable. The inquest held by Esquire Jordan developed very strong evidence against Ritter, and a verdict charging him with the murder was returned. It was proven that he had asked if buzzards ever ate human flesh, and that he had once told his wife, soon after the girl's disappearance, that he was afraid some one had ravished and murdered her. Beside this evidence it was found that a piece of rope which had been used in strangling the girl, was cut from a piece found in Ritter's house after his arrest, and footsteps found in the soft earth near the place where the murder was committed were exactly the size of those his shoes would make.

After the inquest, Sunday, Ritter was brought here and placed in jail. Frequent threats to lynch him were made by the people, both white and black, who live in the neighborhood where the crime was committed, and ever since his arrest the question of summary vengeance has been freely discussed. The colored portion of the murdered girl's friends were especially indignant at the crime and the storm that for three days has been brewing, broke suddenly, yet quietly, this morning and the human fiend was made to suffer the penalty of his hellish crime.

About 1 o'clock, while the Jailer, Elliott Johnson, and his deputy were soundly sleeping, they were awakened by a rapping at the jail door, and on inquiring what was wanted were informed by parties on the outside that they had a prisoner whom they wished taken care of. The Jailer at once opened the door, only to find himself seized

and held by the powerful grasp of several determined men, who presented pistols and guns at his head, saying, however, they did not wish to hurt him, but wanted the murderer, Ritter. Leaving a guard over the Jailer the deputy was seized, the keys taken from him and the door to the guard-room opened. Finding the cell occupied by Ritter, he was dragged forth and taken outside the jail. Arriving at the gate of the jail-yard the Jailer, his deputy and Judge J. C. Averitt and Joseph Adams, who had also been captured by the mob, were released. Mr. Elliott seemed anxious to do his duty and prevent the mob from lynching Ritter, if possible, but in response to his inquiry Judge Averett informed him that he could do nothing, the mob was too strong and seemed capable of carrying out the plans they had laid.

The mob was very quiet, indulged in little talking, and successfully prevented a general alarm by capturing the Marshal and policemen before the jail was visited. Marshal Galloway was held under guard at the Baptist church, and the other officers at the station-house.

After releasing the Jailer and others, the mob, which was composed of between fifty and sixty masked men, took up their march, and leaving the city about a mile behind, found a convenient sassafras tree, and without waste of time the negro fiend was launched into eternity. The crowd then quietly dispersed, leaving the dead body swinging to the tree, a ghastly warning to all that outrage and murder would not be tolerated in Henderson county. Most of the lynchers were negroes, but the number of whites were sufficient to show that others than the murdered girl's race were determined to see her cruel murder avenged.

The body was cut down this morning and an inquest held, and a verdict returned in accordance with the facts. None of the lynchers are known, and the lynching meets with such general approval among all classes that no special effort will be made to discover them. Ritter was about thirty years of age, and leaves a wife, who it is said he frequently threatened to murder.
